Kaggle Twitter Sentiment Analysis

hbmaclean

2025-08-22

1 Introduction

Below is a description of the Twitter Sentiment Analysis Dataset from Kaggle.

Overview

This is an entity-level sentiment analysis dataset of twitter. Given a message and an entity, the task is to judge the sentiment of the message about the entity. There are three classes in this dataset: Positive, Negative and Neutral. We regard messages that are not relevant to the entity (i.e. Irrelevant) as Neutral.

Usage

Please use twitter_training.csv as the training set and twitter_validation.csv as the validation set. Top 1 classification accuracy is used as the metric.

2 Importing Packages

library(data.frame.X)
install_packages(c(
    'curl', 'stringr', 'dplyr', 'tidyr', 'caret', 'tibble', 'kableExtra', 'DT',
    'syuzhet', 'ranger', 'randomForest', 'devtools'
))

install_github('munoztd0/reprtree')
eval(substitute(library(pkg), list(pkg='reprtree')))
library(reprtree)

set.seed(45245)

3 Fetching the Data

In this case, the data is pre-partitioned into training and validation. This downloads the zip and extracts and reads each CSV into a data.frame. Given the note in the data description above, this also mutates “irrelevant” to “neutral”.

fetch_data <- function() {
    options(timeout = 120)
    url <- paste0(
        'https://www.kaggle.com/api/v1/datasets/download/',
        'jp797498e/twitter-entity-sentiment-analysis'
    )
    tmp <- tempfile()
    curl_download(url, tmp)
    cols <- c('id', 'entity', 'sentiment', 'content')
    train_df <<- as.data.frame(
        read.csv(
            unz(tmp, 'twitter_training.csv'),
            header = FALSE,
            col.names = cols
        )
    ) |>
        mutate(sentiment = ifelse(sentiment == 'Irrelevant', 'Neutral', sentiment))

    test_df <<- as.data.frame(
        read.csv(
            unz(tmp, 'twitter_validation.csv'),
            header = FALSE,
            col.names = cols
        )
    ) |>
        mutate(sentiment = ifelse(sentiment == 'Irrelevant', 'Neutral', sentiment))

}
fetch_data()
sample_n(test_df, 5) |> union_all(sample_n(train_df, 5)) |>
    datatable(rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = 't', pageLength = nrow(.data)))

train_df  <- distinct(train_df)

4.2 PCA, Correlation, and Variation

With the three remaining columns, it is clear that the tweet content bears all significant variability and predictive power - I will not even look at PCA, correlation, or variation.

However, I assume that one tweet word may have different sentiment values for different entities - e.g. that “murder” is evidently positive for Borderlands, but presumably negative for Amazon, etc. I am assuming a correlation between entity and the sentiments of content, but at a word-level that I cannot simply check with corr. I will call this the entity-effect.

4.3 Simple Classification Check

Here I arbitrarily pick ranger as a classification model and run it as plain as can be (as a function, to be called again later.)

vanilla_classification <- function(.train = train_df, .test = test_df) {
    etime <- system.time(
        fit  <- ranger(factor(sentiment) ~ ., .train)
    )
    pred <- predict(fit, .test)
    
    cols <- c('Class', 'Prevalence', 'Sensitivity', 'Specificity', 'Precision', 'F1')
    .cm  <- confusionMatrix(pred$predictions, factor(.test$sentiment))
    .cm$byClass |>
        as.data.frame() |>
        rownames_to_column(var = 'Class') |>
        select(all_of(cols)) |>
        kable(
            digits  = 3,
            caption = sprintf(
                'Ranger Classification Metrics - Accuracy %%%.2f; ranger time %.2f(s)',
                .cm$overall[['Accuracy']]*100,
                etime['elapsed']
            )
        ) |>
        kable_styling(
            bootstrap_options = 'bordered',
            full_width = FALSE,
            position = 'left'
        )
}
vanilla_classification()
Ranger Classification Metrics - Accuracy %58.10; ranger time 12.12(s)
Class Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1
Class: Negative 0.266 0.417 0.928 0.677 0.516
Class: Neutral 0.457 0.799 0.488 0.568 0.664
Class: Positive 0.277 0.379 0.878 0.544 0.447

Almost 60% - almost twice the chance of guessing; with an interesting imbalance between sensitivity and specificity.

5 Tweet Content - Lexicon Sentiments

The tweet content looks pretty messy, especially URLs (without protocol, and often broken up by white space, e.g. “dlvr.it / RMTrgF”. Before attempting to clean up with regular expressions, I’ll see how I fare with the data as-is.

In my coursework, I learned of tidytext, and its unnest_tokens, stop_words and get_sentiments to extract tokens/words from a string/column, omit those of little value, and get a “sentiment” for each via one of several lexicons. That was a fine way of teaching what is involved, but in reviewing for this task I found Sentiment Analysis (Lexicons) and a means for getting one sentiment for an entire block of text.

I try that below - getting one sentiment per tweet, from four lexicons. I also calculate a normalized consensus sentiment, deviating slightly from the approach in the article.

train_df <- train_df |>
    mutate(
        bing      = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'bing'),
        afinn     = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'afinn'),
        nrc       = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'nrc'),
        syuzhet   = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'syuzhet'),
        consensus = sign(
            sign(bing) + sign(afinn) + sign(nrc) + sign(syuzhet)
        )
    )

test_df <- test_df |>
    mutate(
        bing      = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'bing'),
        afinn     = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'afinn'),
        nrc       = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'nrc'),
        syuzhet   = syuzhet::get_sentiment(content, method = 'syuzhet'),
        consensus = sign(
            sign(bing) + sign(afinn) + sign(nrc) + sign(syuzhet)
        )
    )

And now to see what difference that made:

vanilla_classification()
Ranger Classification Metrics - Accuracy %81.60; ranger time 28.17(s)
Class Prevalence Sensitivity Specificity Precision F1
Class: Negative 0.266 0.789 0.955 0.864 0.825
Class: Neutral 0.457 0.869 0.814 0.797 0.831
Class: Positive 0.277 0.755 0.931 0.807 0.780

Much improved accuracy; much better balanced sensitivity and specificity; and/but longer runtime, as expected.

Note:

  • syuzhet also supports a stanford lexicon, for which you must install coreNLP and provide its path via ‘path_to_tagger’.
  • Evidently “syuzhet” is a Russian term for “plot” or “storyline”.

5.1 PCA and Correlation!

With the additional columns, PCA (prcomp) and Correlation (cor) get more interesting. Granted, there are not many columns, but two PCs account for 85% of the overall variance.

pca_plot(train_df, pct = .85, which = 'bar')

Two columns, content and entity, have a 97% correlation. I had already hoped that content is unnecessary with the additional sentiment columns. bing, syuzhet, and afinn all correlate strongly (80+%), nrc appears to be an outsider. Alas, evidently nothing correlates strongly with sentiment.

corr_plot(train_df)

Conclusion: pca and corr may be good preProcess options for train. Defaults for preProcess are thresh = .95 for pca and cutoff = .9 for corr. I will also consider dropping nrc, or at least omitting it via formula; and the same with content.

6 Data Cleanup

Here I convert the remaining non-numeric data to numbers; check whether content is still necessary given the summarized lexicon sentiments; whether all the new lexicon sentiment columns are necessary; and check again for resulting duplicates.

6.1 Making it Numeric

I have cycled through this process numerous times. Once, dropping content had comparable accuracy, so I did. Another time, it lowered accuracy by %10 so I did not - but then hit the 16GB vector limit. Here I drop it regardless, and then convert entitity and sentiment to numeric.

While at it, I round syuzhet to three decimals, which in turn introduces tens of duplicates.

unq_sentiments <- unique(c(train_df$sentiment, test_df$sentiment))
unq_entities   <- unique(c(train_df$entity, test_df$entity))

train_df <- train_df |> mutate(
    content   = NULL,
    sentiment = match(sentiment, unq_sentiments) -2,
    entity    = match(entity, unq_entities),
    syuzhet   = round(syuzhet, 3)
)
test_df <-test_df |> mutate(
    content   = NULL,
    sentiment = match(sentiment, unq_sentiments) -2,
    entity    = match(entity, unq_entities),
    syuzhet   = round(syuzhet, 3)
)

7 Initial Multi-Model Framework

Here I create functions for making predictions, calculating accuracy, running individual models, tracking results, and easily running them all together. The goal is to run numerous models and then narrow down to the most accurate one or few.

7.1 Predictions and Accuracy

Below are functions to make predictions and calculate accuracy, using the ellipsis argument to allow model nuances to be passed in.

predictions <- function(model, test_df, type = 'class') {
    tryCatch({
        .pred <- predict(model, test_df, type = type)
    }, 
    error = function(e) {
        print(c(Model = model, error = e))
    },
    finally = {
        if(!is.atomic(.pred)) {
            .pred <- .pred$predictions
        }
        return(.pred)
    })
}

accuracy <- function(model, test_df, ...) {
    tryCatch({
        .pred <- predictions(model, test_df, ...)
        .cm   <- confusionMatrix(.pred, as.factor(test_df$sentiment))
    },
    error = function(e) {
        print(c(Model = model, error = e))
    },
    finally = {
        if (!exists('.cm')) {
            return(NA)
        }
        else {
            return(round(100*.cm$overall[['Accuracy']],2))
        }
    })
}

7.2 Formula and Models

And here, a basic formula; and a function for each model plus the type for the underlying predict - generally ‘class’ or ‘response’.

fc <- as.formula(factor(sentiment) ~ .)
models <- list(
    ranger       = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { ranger(...) },
        TYPE = 'response'
    ),
    randomForest = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { randomForest(..., ntree = 20) },
        TYPE = 'response'
    ),
    knn3         = list(
        FUNC = function(...) { knn3(...) },
        TYPE = 'class'
    )
)

Notes:

  1. Originally, I had six models - the above three plus multinom, native_bayes, and avNNet. I eventually pared it down to shave execution time.
  2. ranger was uniquely problematic here. Originally, rather than TYPE, I set this up as extraArgs with a value of c(type = 'class') for example, or NULL if the underlying default was sufficient. But ranger gave, Error: Expecting a single value: [extent=0] when extraArgs was NULL; and Error: Not compatible with requested type: [type=character; target=logical] when extraArgs was c(type = 'response'). All other models behaved as expected, with a key-value pair or NULL.

7.3 Model Runner

Finally, a function to actually run the models and accumulate metrics.

.run_model <- function(cfg, .formula, .train, .test) {
    FUNC <- cfg$FUNC
    TYPE <- cfg$TYPE
    accuracy(
        get("FUNC")(.formula, .train),
        .test, type = TYPE
    )
}

run_models <- function(
        .models  = models,
        .formula = fc,
        .train   = train_df,
        .test    = test_df
    ) {
        results <- sapply(names(.models), function(model) {
            .run_model(.models[[model]], .formula, .train, .test)
        })
        names(results) <- names(.models)
        return(results)
}

7.4 Metrics Summary

Below, a function to display the metrics. At the moment, the expectation is that the named vector from run_models will be bound with an initial column of meaningful labels.

display_summary <- function(.data) {
    .data |>
        dplyr::rename(` ` = c(1)) |>
        datatable(
            rownames = FALSE,
            options  = list(
                dom        = 't',
                pageLength = nrow(.data)
            )
        )
}

8 Second Multi-Model Framework - train()

8.1 Models and Tuning

I will stick with ranger and add in Rborist and treebag.

First, I define a list of NULL trControl, tuneGrid, and preProcess objects (and maybe extraArgs, but there is a rant coming up.)

train_config <- list(
    ranger = list(
        trControl  = NULL,
        tuneGrid   = NULL,
        preProcess = NULL,
        extraArgs  = NULL
    ),
    Rborist = list(
        trControl  = NULL,
        tuneGrid   = NULL,
        preProcess = NULL,
        extraArgs  = NULL
    ),
    treebag = list(
        trControl  = NULL,
        tuneGrid   = NULL,
        preProcess = NULL,
        extraArgs  = NULL
    )
)

Note:

  • Here again, I initially tried many more models in addition to the above: svmRadial, mlp, xgbTree, gamLoess, rocc, glmnet, vglmContRatio, RFlda, and lssvmRadial, chosen arbitrarily from this caret list - but they all underperformed by 30% or more, and the execution time was intolerable.

8.2 Running the Models via Train

Here I write a function to generically execute a model via train and capture its accuracy. Arguments allow for alternate data sets, formula, model list, trControl and lists of tuneGrid objects.

.train_model  <- function(
        model, cfg, .formula, .train, .test, bestTune,
       .trControl = NULL, .preProcess = NULL
) {
    tryCatch({
        fit <- (function(...) {
            caret::train(
                .formula,
                method     = model,
                data       = .train,
                trControl  = dplyr::coalesce(
                    .trControl,
                    trainControl(
                        method = 'repeatedcv',
                        number = 2,
                        p      = .5
                    )
                ),
                tuneGrid   = cfg$tuneGrid,
                preProcess = .preProcess,
                ...
            )
        })() # ideally, (...) 
    }, error = function(e) {
        print(c(Model = model, error = e))
    },
    finally = {
        if (exists('fit')) {
            if (bestTune) {
                print(c(Model = model, bestTune = fit$bestTune))
            }
            return(accuracy(fit, .test, type = 'raw'))
        }
    })
}

train_models <- function(
    .config       = train_config,
    .formula      = fc,
    .train        = train_df,
    .test         = test_df,
    bestTune      = FALSE,
    .trControl    = NULL,
    .preProcess   = NULL
) {
    results <- sapply(names(.config), function(model) {
        .train_model(
            model, .config[[model]], .formula, .train, .test,
            bestTune, .trControl, .preProcess
        )
    })
    names(results) <- names(.config)
    return(results)
}

Notes:

  1. The inner, anonymous function remains setup to accept extra arguments. I struggled mightily to send SOMETHING (key-value pair(s)) or NOTHING (i.e. not NULL). The only workaround so far is calling it with or without extra arguments via if/else, defeating the purpose of the ellipsis.
  2. I also got burned terribly here. Prior to wrapping in tryCatch, the function worked in most cases but died with some models for some parameters. Within tryCatch, I was getting nothing but NA - and a lot of them, even distilled down to one model. It seems tryCatch requires an explicit return statement, and that without it I was getting the value of the finally block…?

8.4 Tuning the Models

Now I look for improvements via tuneGrid, preProcess, and trainControl options.

8.4.1 tuneGrid

I started with tuneGrid and ran the models once without any customization and captured their out-of-the-box best tuneGrid values; then repeated with various ranges around those values. This remains a manual and tedious step, and generally not very effective. Below are the values I settled upon after several iterations of nothing exciting.

    ranger = list(

            mtry          = 3,

        )
    ),
    Rborist = list(
        tuneGrid = expand.grid(
            predFixed = 2,
            minNode   = 3
        )
    ),
    treebag = list(
    )
)

This is terribly inconsistent, despite setting seed. Ironically, treebag tends to change most, in either direction, despite not having a tuneGrid. At least once, ranger plummeted 26% despite its tuneGrid permutations including the values of the initial bestTune! At any rate, there is generally not enough movement to consider worthwhile.

8.4.2 trainControl

Here I nullify the trainGrid settings and look at various trainControl methods.

train_config <- list(
    ranger = list(
        tuneGrid = NULL
    ),
    Rborist = list(
        tuneGrid = NULL
    ),
    treebag = list(
        tuneGrid = NULL
    )
)

boot_results <- bind_rows(
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'boot', number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'boot632', number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'optimism_boot', number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'boot_all', number = 2))
)

cv_results <- bind_rows(
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'cv', p = .5, repeats = 2, number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'repeatedcv', p = .5, repeats = 2, number = 2)),
    train_models(.trControl = trainControl(
        method = 'LGOCV', p = .5, repeats = 2, number = 2))
)

train_summary <- bind_cols(
    c(
        'boot', 'boot632', 'optimism_boot', 'boot_all',
        'cv', 'repeatedcv', 'LGOCV'
    ),
    bind_rows(boot_results, cv_results)
)

display_summary(train_summary)

Note:

  • There are also ‘adaptive_boot’, ‘adaptive_cv’, and ‘adaptive_LGOCV’. They produced errors - adaptive$min should be less than 2, and then adaptive$min should be greater than 1, and finally For adaptive resampling, there needs to be more than one tuning parameter for evaluation, with adaptive = list(min = 2, ...), min = 1, and min = 1.1. Infuriatingly, running the same on the command line worked. But for the good, this inspired tryCatch.

Conclusion - Again, not enough movement to consider worthwhile.

8.4.3 preProcess

Now I try various preProcess methods. I do not try scale or center, which I’ve already simulated; nor cor since I already omitted content, half of the strongest correlating pair.

pre_results <- bind_rows(
    train_models(.preProcess = c('BoxCox')),
    train_models(.preProcess = c('YeoJohnson')),
    train_models(.preProcess = c('expoTrans')),
    train_models(.preProcess = c('spatialSign')),
    train_models(.preProcess = c('pca'))
)
## note: only 2 unique complexity parameters in default grid. Truncating the grid to 2 .
## 
## note: only 2 unique complexity parameters in default grid. Truncating the grid to 2 .
pre_summary <- bind_cols(
    c('BoxCox', 'YeoJohnson', 'expoTrans', 'spatialSign', 'pca'),
    pre_results
)

display_summary(pre_summary)

Notes:

There are numerous other preProcess methods:

  • I ruled out zv and nzv, as any column here with little variance is expected.

  • knnImpute, bagImpute, and medianImpute are not applicable as there are no missing values.

  • I looked further into conditionalX. Its description in preProcess help left me uncertain, and I found a fuller description alongside nearZeroVar. In summary, it looks at the distribution of each predictor conditioned on the levels of the outcome, and identifies any predictor that is sparse within groups of the outcome.

    I ran checkConditionalX as follows - and no predictor was identified. (I will add this to my early analysis checklist, along with outliers, NAs, duplicates, etc .)

    checkConditionalX(train_df |> select(-c(sentiment)), train_df$sentiment)
    ## integer(0)

9 Final Validation

The three models were close enough. Only ranger improved from baseline, about equally for preProcess and trainControl. randomForest and treebag moved so slightly I would discount it to randomness.

train_config <- list(
    ranger = list(
        tuneGrid = NULL
    ),
    Rborist = list(
        tuneGrid = NULL
    ),
    treebag = list(
        tuneGrid = NULL
    )
)

final_results <- train_models(
    .train = train_org,
    .test  = test_org
)

final_summary <- bind_cols(
    c('baseline', 'bestTune', 'trainControl', 'preProcess', 'finalValidation'),
    bind_rows(
        baselines,
        bestTunes,
        c(
            ranger  = max(train_summary[['ranger']]),
            Rborist = max(train_summary[['Rborist']]),
            treebag = max(train_summary[['treebag']])
        ),
        c(
            ranger  = max(pre_results[['ranger']]),
            Rborist = max(pre_results[['Rborist']]),
            treebag = max(pre_results[['treebag']])
        ),
        final_results
    )
)

display_summary(final_summary)

10 Conclusions

  1. The winner is inconclusive; the numbers changes per run. (Did I NOT set seed?) I only see Python solutions on Kaggle, and they generally have train accuracy in the mid-90s and validation accuracy in the mid-80s. This Rmd matches that, albeit erratically…
  2. My primary goal was continued learning:
    • Paragraph-based sentiments was the big lesson.
    • I gained more comfort with tryCatch and ..., but both came with surprises. I need to learn more, especially whether there is an idiomatic method of, for example, reading optional parameters/values from a config file and passing to an ellipses. Perhaps it is just that simple, but my experience here says otherwise.
    • I had a note to myself to try dtree but when trying to install it I see that Package ‘dtree’ was removed from the CRAN repository.
  3. I had many troubles with this project - in addition to lengthy execution times against the full training set:
    • Once, transitioning between Visual and Source editing modes, the closing backticks were removed from almost every code block, preventing Visual mode.
    • Many times, a block of code failed or ran extremely slowly in RStudio but fine in the console - or vice versa.
    • Once, manually running code blocks from the top down, each kickoff scrolled the document back to the top; forcing me to scroll further and further down to run the next block. What is that?!
    • Already mentioned, accuracy changed wildly without plausible explanation, despite seed. Against the partitioned halves, accuracy fluctuated from the mid-60s to mid-90s?!
    • I very often had to run code blocks twice in this Rmd: Often, a spurious second box of (empty) output is created, and disappears on subsequent run. Occasionally, the desired output is cropped and unscrollable - and self-corrects on a subsequent run. Occasionally, there is no output for no apparent reason - in which case I can often run just the output-producing line(s), proving that everything else worked.
  4. Once again, most effort was for naught, other than learning. The only thing that helped in a measurable way was the one obvious need - calculating sentiments.

12 Appendix

12.1 RandomForest Decision Tree

I like to end with a look at a model’s decision tree. I’ve never seen one with such symmetry! I can imagine the difficult choices.

fit <- randomForest(
    factor(sentiment) ~ .,
    train_df,
    ntree = 20
)   
simplest_tree <- which.min(fit$forest$ndbigtree)
fit$forest$xbestsplit <- round(fit$forest$xbestsplit, 2)  # 'digits' workaround
plot.getTree(
    fit,
    k     = simplest_tree,
    depth = 6,
    main  = sprintf(
        'RandomForest Decision Tree - Accuracy %.2f',
        accuracy(fit, test_df)
    )
)

12.2 Case-Specific Random Forests

Reading further about ranger, I noticed csrf and thought I’d try it. Alas, running against the full train/validation sets gives, Error in table(data, reference, dnn = dnn, …) : all arguments must have the same length. That seems odd - is it uncommon to have different sized data sets…?

pred <- csrf(
    factor(sentiment) ~ .,
    training_data = train_df,
    test_data     = test_df,
    params1       = list(num.trees = 50, mtry = 4),
    params2       = list(num.trees = 5)
)

cm <- confusionMatrix(pred, factor(test_df$sentiment))
cm$overall[['Accuracy']]
## [1] 0.8445435
